Party Ideas & Guides

What to Put in Children's Party Bags Without the Sugar Hit

If you are working out what to put in children's party bags and you would rather not send twelve children home on a sugar high, the answer is a small number of useful things rather than a handful of lollies. I aim for three or four items per bag, built around something to make, something to play with and at most one treat.

Three or four items per bag Low sugar ideas by type Keeping the bags equal

That keeps the cost sensible, keeps the other parents on side, and gives the children something that lasts longer than the drive home. If the bags are the last thing on your list and you are still working out the entertainment for a birthday party, sort that first, because the bags are the easy part.

Why the low sugar approach is worth it

Party bags are a small gift, but they land at the worst possible moment. The children have already had a couple of hours of running and plenty of food. Adding a bag of lollies hands every parent a difficult evening, and most of those bags get quietly confiscated in the car anyway.

There is also the practical side. Lollies and chocolate melt in an Australian December, so anything you buy on the Thursday can arrive as a sticky mess on the Saturday. Non food items survive the heat, the car and being left in a bag for three days.

The other quiet benefit is dietary needs. Once food is out of the equation you no longer need to track who cannot have nuts, dairy, gluten or artificial colours. None of this means the bags have to be dull. Children care about getting something that is theirs, and what it is matters much less than adults expect.

Stationery and craft items

This category does the most work. Small stationery items look generous, cost very little each and get used for weeks.

Think stickers, temporary tattoos, a small notepad, a printed pencil, mini erasers in fun shapes, washi tape or a short set of textas. Craft items go further again, so a bead and string kit, a paint your own plaster shape, modelling dough or a simple sewing card all work.

The trick is one item with something to do rather than three things that sit in the bag. A paint your own figurine beats five loose pencils, because it gives the child an activity for the afternoon rather than an object. Match the craft to the age, since beading and small pieces suit school age children while under fives do better with dough, chunky chalk or stickers.

Nature and activity items

This group suits the Australian summer, because almost everything in it sends the children back outside.

Seed packets are a favourite, especially fast growing things like sunflowers, beans or herbs. A small pot or peat disc alongside turns it into a whole activity. Origami paper with one printed instruction sheet works for older children, and so does a paper plane kit or a simple kite.

Bubbles belong here too, along with a skipping rope, chalk for the driveway, a magnifying glass or a small bug catcher. Sand and water toys suit a summer party, and a beach ball or frisbee makes a decent single item bag on its own.

If you want the take home to feel like part of the day rather than an afterthought, think about who is already at the party, because a balloon twister can hand each child something to take home as they leave and save you filling that slot in the bag at all.

Fidget and sensory toys

Fidget and sensory items give the most excitement for the least cost, and they are genuinely useful for children who need something to do with their hands.

Pop tubes, stretchy noodles, squish balls, putty, liquid motion timers and simple puzzle cubes all go down well, and sensory items are often the thing still being played with a month later. Check the sizing before you buy in bulk, because small stretchy and squishy toys come apart or get bitten through, so choose larger single piece items for the youngest guests.

Classic novelty toys

There is a reason the old favourites keep turning up. Yo yos, spinning tops, bubble wands, kaleidoscopes, slinkies, maze puzzles, wind up toys, finger puppets and a pack of snap cards all hold up.

Novelty toys tend to be the item children show each other at the door, which is half the fun. Choose one hero item and keep everything else small, rather than filling the bag with five cheap things that will not survive the week. Books work the same way, and a single thin activity, sticker or puzzle book makes a respectable bag with almost nothing else in it.

A small number of consumables, done well

Taking the sugar out does not mean taking everything out. One treat per bag is plenty, and choosing it well makes the bag feel like a party bag.

A single decent biscuit, a small popcorn bag or a packet of plain or fruit based snacks all do the job. One item means a parent can hand it over without a negotiation, and it will not melt into the stickers if you keep the bags out of the sun. Leave the wrapper on so the ingredients are visible, and if several guests have dietary needs, drop food from the bags entirely and put a little more into the toy.

Age appropriateness and the choking hazard question

This is the part worth slowing down for. The ACCC Product Safety service advises that small objects can pose a choking hazard to children under three, and that toys should be chosen according to the age labelling on the packaging. If younger siblings will be at the party, and at a summer party they usually are, small items such as marbles, beads, bouncy balls and anything with removable parts should not go into a bag a toddler can reach.

The easiest fix is two versions of the bag. Make the standard bag for the birthday guests, and a handful of toddler safe bags with larger single piece items, a board book or crayons. Keep them separated and hand them out deliberately rather than from one pile.

Balloons deserve a note of their own. The ACCC Product Safety service identifies uninflated and broken balloons as a choking risk for young children, so keep them out of any bag a toddler can reach.

Keeping the bags equal, and how many items to use

Children compare bags, and they will do it in the hallway before they reach the front door, so identical bags save a great deal of bother. If you want to vary anything, vary only colour and let every child choose as they leave. Two versions split by age is fine too, as long as the difference is clearly about age rather than about who got the better bag.

Three to four items is the sweet spot, and it breaks down like this:

What goes into a three or four item party bag
SlotWhat to put in it
The hero itemOne better thing: a craft kit, an activity book, a sensory toy or a beach ball
A craft or activity itemSeed packets, origami paper, dough, chalk or a bead and string kit
A small toyA yo yo, spinning top, bubble wand, finger puppet or pack of snap cards
At most one treatA single biscuit, a small popcorn bag or a plain or fruit based snack

Any more than that and the bag stops feeling considered and starts feeling like clearing out a drawer. Write the children's names on the bags if you have the guest list, because it stops arguments and stops bags walking out the door twice. Keep a couple of spares for the sibling who comes along and the guest you did not expect.

Frequently asked questions

What are some good ideas for a party bag for a 7 year old?

Seven year olds are ready for a bit of challenge, so a small craft kit, a puzzle book, a puzzle cube, friendship bracelet string, a yo yo or a pack of snap cards all work well. At this age the item they can do something with beats the item they just own, so one activity plus a sticker sheet and a single treat makes a solid bag.

What are some good party favours that are not junk?

Seed packets, craft kits, a thin activity or sticker book, art supplies such as chalk or textas, a sensory toy, bubbles or outdoor play items such as a skipping rope or frisbee all avoid the throwaway feeling. The test I use is whether the item will still be in the house in a fortnight.

What should I put in goodie bags for 8 year olds?

Eight year olds like things that feel a little grown up, so a proper pen or notebook, a card game, a puzzle, a build it yourself kit, a keyring or a sports item such as a tennis ball goes down better than novelty toys. One slightly better single item is more successful than four small ones at this age.
